finding.claim: deleteAccount never enforces authorization: canDelete(u, a) is called but its boolean result is discarded, so any caller (including non-admin non-owners) can delete any account by id.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled `id` (path parameter of DELETE /accounts/{id}) and any authenticated `User u` (non-admin, not the owner). Precondition: caller holds any valid User object.
finding.sink: src/AccountService.java:23 accounts.remove(id) - destructive state change on an account the caller does not own.

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) entry point; u and id are caller-controlled.
Loads Account a for attacker-supplied id; no existence or ownership check here.
canDelete(u, a) evaluated, return value ignored. No if/throw wraps it, so the authorization decision has no effect.
accounts.remove(id) executes unconditionally, deleting the target account.

finding.guards_checked: (1) canDelete at line 9-11 is correct in isolation (admin OR owner) but its result is unused at line 22. (2) assertCanDelete (line 13-17) is the enforcing wrapper and is NOT called in deleteAccount; it is only used in closeAccount. (3) No caller-side check is visible in this file; the route/controller that invokes deleteAccount is not in the repo, so an upstream authz filter cannot be ruled out from this code alone and would need confirming. (4) Null account: for a missing id, a is null; admin short-circuits to true, non-admin NPEs at line 10 - neither prevents removal of an existing account by a non-owner.
finding.severity_note: High: broken object-level authorization (IDOR / CWE-285/CWE-639) on a destructive operation. Likely the intended code was `assertCanDelete(u, a);`.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. canDelete (src/AccountService.java:9-11) is correct in isolation, but its boolean is discarded as a bare statement at line 22, so nothing is enforced before accounts.remove(id) at line 23. assertCanDelete (lines 13-17) would throw, but deleteAccount never calls it; only closeAccount (line 29) does. No caller or route handler for DELETE /accounts/{id} exists in the repo (the Grep for deleteAccount/DELETE/accounts/ found only this file), so an upstream authz filter cannot be ruled out from this code alone.
verdict.reason: Line 22 calls canDelete(u, a) as a bare statement and discards its result, so accounts.remove(id) at line 23 runs for any User u regardless of ownership or admin status, and no effective control in the repo blocks it. The one caveat is that the HTTP route is not in this repo, so an authz check in a caller outside it would have to be confirmed separately.

finding.claim: closeAccount does not null-check the loaded Account, so for a non-existent id a non-admin gets a NullPointerException while an existing-but-unowned account yields SecurityException, giving an account-existence oracle.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled `id` and a non-admin authenticated `User u`.
finding.sink: src/AccountService.java:29 assertCanDelete -> line 10 a.ownerId() on a null Account; differing exception types/responses reveal whether an id exists.

trace.note: closeAccount(User u, long id) entry point.
accounts.get(id) returns null when id does not exist.
assertCanDelete(u, a) called with a == null.
u.admin() false, so a.ownerId() dereferences null -> NullPointerException (500). For an existing unowned account, SecurityException is thrown instead.

finding.guards_checked: Authorization itself is enforced correctly on this path (assertCanDelete throws for non-owner non-admin). The defect is the missing null handling and the resulting distinguishable failure modes. Exposure depends on whether the HTTP layer maps the exception types to distinct status codes or messages, which is outside this file. Low severity: enumeration of ids only, no state change. Admin path on a missing id silently succeeds at line 30 (no-op remove) rather than erroring, a further inconsistency.
finding.severity_note: Low: information disclosure (account enumeration) via inconsistent error handling; no direct unauthorized write.

verdict.guard_found: None on the closeAccount path. accounts.get(id) at src/AccountService.java:28 returns null for a missing id with no check, and assertCanDelete (line 13-17) only throws SecurityException, so line 10 `a.ownerId()` dereferences null for a non-admin (NPE). The admin path short-circuits at line 10 (u.admin() true) and does not dereference a. No HTTP layer or exception mapper is present in the directory (only src/AccountService.java), so whether the two failure modes are externally distinguishable is not established here.
verdict.reason: At src/AccountService.java:28-29 a missing id yields a null Account that reaches line 10 and throws NullPointerException for a non-admin, while an existing unowned account throws SecurityException at line 15, so the code-level behavior matches the claim; the reachability is by any authenticated low-privilege user, and the oracle only becomes externally visible if the unseen HTTP layer maps these exceptions differently, making this a low-severity information-disclosure defect rather than an authorization bypass.
